_comment: The site map from the build spec, §2, in machine-readable form. `npm run scaffold` turns this into stub pages under src/content/pages/ without ever overwriting a page that already exists. Edit a page's prose in its markdown file; edit its identity (title, track, terms, figure) here and re-run scaffold to check nothing has drifted.

tracks.title: The map of the territory
tracks.purpose: Answer "what markets exist, and why does each one exist at all".

pages.title: What a market is
pages.summary: A market is a mechanism for finding the price at which two people will swap. Everything else is detail about who, where and when.

figure.title: How big is each market, really
figure.source: WFE, BIS Triennial Survey, SIFMA, CoinGecko
figure.series: equity market cap; bond outstandings; FX daily turnover; crypto market cap

pages.title: Goods markets vs financial markets
pages.summary: What changes when the thing being traded can be stored, split, and swapped for an identical copy of itself.

figure.title: Storability and the shape of a price series
figure.series: wheat, electricity, copper spot vs AAPL

pages.title: Asset classes
pages.summary: The conventional partition of tradable things, and why the boundaries sit where they do.

figure.title: Return and volatility by asset class, same axes

pages.title: Equity market vs crypto market
pages.summary: Two markets in the same instrument type, built on opposite institutional assumptions.

figure.title: Volume by hour of day: a listed equity vs BTC

pages.title: Exchange vs OTC
pages.summary: Whether you trade against a book or against a dealer changes the price you get and who knows about it.

figure.title: Share of US equity volume executed off-exchange
figure.series: weekly ATS and OTC volume vs consolidated volume

pages.title: Who is on the other side
pages.summary: The taxonomy of participants, what each is optimising, and which of them is obliged to trade with you.

figure.title: Concentration of US equity ownership

tracks.title: Contracts and instruments
tracks.purpose: The nouns. What an instrument is: a set of state-contingent cash flows.

pages.title: Cash flows and discounting
pages.summary: Every instrument is a promise of money at future dates. Pricing starts by asking what a future pound is worth now.

figure.title: Today's discount curve, built from Treasury par yields
figure.source: US Treasury daily par yield curve

pages.title: Equity
pages.summary: A residual claim on a company: last in line, unlimited upside, and the reason the word "risk" got its modern meaning.

figure.title: Total return vs price return over 30 years
figure.series: index price return vs total return

pages.title: Bonds
pages.summary: A fixed schedule of payments, so that the only interesting questions are the discount rate and whether you get paid at all.

figure.title: Price against yield for a real bond

pages.title: Forwards and futures
pages.summary: Agreeing today on the price of a trade that happens later, and the machinery that makes that promise safe.

figure.title: Futures term structure, and how it moves
figure.series: VIX futures curve; BTC perpetual and quarterly basis

pages.title: Options
pages.summary: The right without the obligation, which is what makes the payoff non-linear and the pricing interesting.

figure.title: A real option chain: payoff at expiry vs price today
figure.series: one index option chain, all strikes at one expiry

pages.title: Swaps and the rest
pages.summary: Exchanging one stream of payments for another — the largest market in the world by notional, and the least visible.

figure.title: Swap rate against government yield: the swap spread
figure.series: swap rates vs Treasury constant maturity

pages.title: Derivatives: what the word actually means
pages.summary: A contract whose value is a function of something else's price. That is the whole definition, and it is why the scary headline numbers are misread.

figure.title: Notional outstanding vs gross market value of OTC derivatives
figure.series: notional amounts outstanding; gross market values

pages.title: Hedging vs speculation vs arbitrage
pages.summary: Three reasons to put on the same trade, distinguished entirely by what you already own.

figure.title: Hedged vs unhedged fuel cost for an airline
figure.series: jet fuel spot; heating oil / crude futures

tracks.title: Market microstructure
tracks.purpose: The verbs. How a price is actually produced, tick by tick.

pages.title: The order book
pages.summary: The list of everything anyone is currently willing to trade, and the rules for matching it. This is where price comes from.

figure.title: Order book depth, live and replayed
figure.series: BTCUSDT L2 book; one NASDAQ name, message-by-message
figure.period: live, plus one full sample session

pages.title: Order types and execution
pages.summary: The instructions you can attach to an order, and what each one costs you.

figure.title: Cost of a market order as a function of its size

pages.title: Liquidity
pages.summary: How much you can trade, how fast, and how far you move the price doing it. Three different questions with one name.

figure.title: Spread and top-of-book depth by time of day

pages.title: Price formation and impact
pages.summary: Trading moves the price against you. The shape of that relationship is one of the most robust empirical laws in finance.

figure.title: Price response to signed volume
figure.series: BTCUSDT aggregated trades, signed by taker side

pages.title: Market makers and adverse selection
pages.summary: Quoting both sides is profitable until the person hitting your quote knows something you don't.

figure.title: Effective spread against realised spread

pages.title: Latency and the arms race
pages.summary: When the queue is priced in microseconds, speed becomes a capital expenditure.

figure.title: Time between consecutive book updates

tracks.title: The statistical anatomy of prices
tracks.purpose: The econophysics core. This is where the physics background pays immediately.

pages.title: Returns
pages.summary: Prices are not the observable; changes in log price are. Getting this right fixes half the confusions downstream.

figure.title: The same series as price, log price, and returns

pages.title: Fat tails
pages.summary: Large moves are not rare accidents at the edge of a bell curve. They are a power law, and they dominate everything you care about.

figure.title: Survival function of normalised returns, log–log axes
figure.series: S&P 500 (^SPX), EUR/USD, BTCUSDT — daily log returns, normalised by sample volatility

pages.title: Volatility clustering
pages.summary: Returns are almost unpredictable; their magnitudes are extremely predictable. That asymmetry is the central empirical fact about prices.

figure.title: Autocorrelation of returns against autocorrelation of absolute returns

pages.title: Scale invariance
pages.summary: Aggregate returns over longer windows and the distribution slowly becomes Gaussian — but far more slowly than independence would predict.

figure.title: Kurtosis as a function of aggregation scale
figure.series: returns aggregated from 1 minute to 1 month

pages.title: The leverage effect
pages.summary: Prices fall and volatility rises; prices rise and volatility drifts down. The asymmetry is real, and it is not symmetric across asset classes.

figure.title: Correlation between returns and future volatility

pages.title: Correlations
pages.summary: A correlation matrix estimated from a few hundred observations of a few hundred assets is mostly noise, and random matrix theory tells you exactly how much.

figure.title: Empirical eigenvalue spectrum against Marchenko-Pastur

pages.title: Is the market efficient?
pages.summary: Efficiency is not a yes-or-no property. The useful version is: which currents are exploitable after costs, and at what horizon.

figure.title: Variance ratio against lag: the signature plot

tracks.title: Pricing and risk
tracks.purpose: The standard machinery, taught the way a physicist should meet it.

pages.title: No-arbitrage and replication
pages.summary: If two portfolios pay the same in every state of the world, they cost the same today. Almost all of pricing is that sentence applied carefully.

figure.title: How tightly does put-call parity actually hold
figure.series: one index option chain, matched call and put strikes

pages.title: Bachelier and Black-Scholes
pages.summary: A hedging argument, not a forecast: if you can trade continuously, the option's risk cancels and only volatility survives.

figure.title: Residual P&L of a delta-hedged option
figure.series: one index option, hedged daily to expiry

pages.title: The volatility surface
pages.summary: One number per option, plotted against strike and maturity, and it is emphatically not flat. That shape is the market's correction to the model.

figure.title: Implied volatility surface, and VIX against realised
figure.series: index option implied vols; VIX history

pages.title: Portfolio construction
pages.summary: Mean-variance optimisation is an inverse problem with a badly conditioned operator, and it fails in exactly the way that predicts.

figure.title: The efficient frontier, in sample and out

pages.title: Risk measures
pages.summary: Summarising a distribution by one number, and the specific ways each summary lies to you.

figure.title: VaR exceedances through 2008 and March 2020

pages.title: Position sizing
pages.summary: Given an edge, how much to bet is a separate and harder question than whether you have one.

figure.title: Growth rate against betting fraction on a real series

tracks.title: Economics
tracks.purpose: The macro layer, with the same discipline. Backbone data source: FRED.

pages.title: What GDP actually measures
pages.summary: An accounting identity for produced output over a period, not a measure of wealth, welfare, or anything anyone directly observes.

figure.title: Contributions to GDP growth: C, I, G, NX

pages.title: Money and inflation
pages.summary: The quantity theory is an identity plus two heroic assumptions, and 2021 was the cleanest test of it in forty years.

figure.title: M2 growth against CPI inflation, with 2021-23 marked

pages.title: Interest rates and central banks
pages.summary: A central bank sets one overnight rate. Everything that matters happens in how the rest of the curve responds.

figure.title: Policy rate against 2-year and 10-year yields

pages.title: The yield curve
pages.summary: The term structure of interest rates, and the most-watched recession indicator that nobody can fully explain.

figure.title: Curve inversions against NBER recessions

pages.title: Labour, output, prices
pages.summary: The supposed trade-off between unemployment and inflation, and what its instability tells you about macro modelling.

figure.title: The Phillips curve, coloured by decade

pages.title: Exchange rates
pages.summary: The one price where two countries' entire monetary conditions meet, and where the textbook parities fail most visibly.

figure.title: Carry trade P&L and the CIP basis after 2008
figure.series: FX spot and forward points, policy rate differentials

pages.title: Credit and the cycle
pages.summary: Recessions are usually credit events. The spread is a price, a forecast, and a feedback loop at the same time.

figure.title: High-yield spread against recessions

pages.title: Economics as a complex system
pages.summary: Agents that copy each other produce the stylised facts of real markets without any of the equilibrium apparatus.

figure.title: A herding model against a real return series
figure.series: Kirman ant model output vs equity index returns

tracks.title: Plumbing and institutions
tracks.purpose: What actually happens after "trade done". Almost never taught, always assumed.

pages.title: Clearing and settlement
pages.summary: The days between agreeing a trade and owning the asset, and the institution that stands in the middle so you never learn your counterparty's name.

figure.title: Settlement fails in US Treasuries
figure.series: primary dealer fails to deliver and receive

pages.title: Margin and leverage
pages.summary: How much capital you must post to hold a position, and why that number is the real constraint on every leveraged strategy.

figure.title: Margin debt against the market it finances
figure.series: margin debt outstanding vs index level

pages.title: Funding
pages.summary: Where the cash actually comes from overnight, and what happens on the days it doesn't.

figure.title: SOFR against the policy rate, with the spikes

pages.title: Wrappers
pages.summary: Funds, ETFs and notes are containers, not assets. What matters is the mechanism that keeps the container's price near its contents.

figure.title: ETF premium and discount to NAV through stress
figure.series: one bond ETF, price vs NAV

pages.title: Regulation
pages.summary: The rules that decide where you may trade, what you must tell people, and which clever idea is a felony.

figure.title: Regulatory regime changes against market structure
figure.series: off-exchange share with regime boundaries marked

pages.title: Crypto plumbing
pages.summary: The same functions — matching, clearing, custody, funding — rebuilt from scratch with different trust assumptions and mostly worse guarantees.

figure.title: Perpetual funding rate against the spot-futures basis
figure.series: BTCUSDT funding rate, mark and index price

tracks.title: How quant research is actually done
tracks.purpose: The applied layer, kept last and kept small so the site stays general.

pages.title: Signals and alpha
pages.summary: A signal is a forecast with a horizon. Everything about its value follows from how fast it decays and how much it can absorb.

figure.title: Information coefficient decay for short-term reversal

pages.title: Backtesting and its pathologies
pages.summary: A backtest is a measurement performed on data you have already looked at, which is a category of experiment physics has strong opinions about.

figure.title: The same strategy in sample and out of sample

pages.title: Costs
pages.summary: Gross Sharpe is a physics problem. Net Sharpe is an engineering problem, and it is the only one that pays.

figure.title: Equity curve as turnover rises
figure.source: Stooq; impact model calibrated in Track 2
figure.series: one signal at several holding periods

pages.title: From research to P&L
pages.summary: The distance between a signal that predicts and a book that makes money, measured in risk model and neutralisation.

figure.title: Factor-neutral against raw returns of one signal
figure.series: one signal, before and after neutralisation
